doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Later careers of Cannonball, Monk and Evans
title: Bill Evans leaving for Verve, Helen Keane and Fantasy
summary: Evans left Riverside for Verve with a buyout, Helen Keane became his producer, and Keepnews later recorded him at the Vanguard.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: him up a notch to a major label, and he was pulled away from us. And I didn’t think anything sensible or helpful or intelligent was done to his career subsequently. Bill Evans also went on to a — although there what happened was he kind of knew that he was kind of good in the sense that even though when Bill first went to Verve, and that was a matter of Bill left Riverside with a year to go on his contract which was because we were in existence, we were starting to have real money problems and frankly Bill had turned into one of the most expensive junkies I ever had to be involved with, represented more of a burden than we really could comfortably handle. I mean I have said this and I’ve written about this before, it’s not anything new, but being his record company, his friend, and his producer all at the same time was a hell of a strain on me. I did not appreciate the way that whole thing came down at the end. And what happened was with a year to go and Creed Taylor was extremely anxious to have Bill as his artist, and bring him over to Verve, so that a buyout kind of thing was arranged. I retained the right to do two more albums with Bill and of the sizable advance that he got from Verve, half of it was in the form of a check to Riverside Records which represented only a partial repayment of what we had over-advanced him. It’s interesting and shows the passage of time. In a sense this is related to what had happened eight years earlier with Riverside buying Monk out of his Prestige contract but the amounts were hugely different. But Bill, what happened there as far as the artistic content, after a very little while something, and I never have felt it was any of my business even knowing, but something was not right in the working relationship between Bill and his producer there, and Bill’s manager, a woman who was very, very important in his life, Helen Keane, took over as Bill’s producer and actually did serve as a producer of the rest of his output. That included a funny period, he also was at Fantasy in the early 70s, and actually I think Helen and I intended to co-produce a live date together. Bill was recorded — well we initially intended to record it at Shelly’s Manne-Hole in Los Angeles but Shelly’s had just moved from its original funky location into the basement of a bank building and there was a big — the air conditioning equipment broke down and the whole floor of the club was covered in about a foot of oil out of the equipment. So we canceled that one out and ended up recording him at the Vanguard and Helen got sick and didn’t make it so I ended up doing that one by myself. So we never did get to co-produce it, which probably was a good idea. But Bill actually was pretty — see Bill knew what he wanted and was pretty insistent on it as Cannon was. But Bill was doing trio albums the rest of his life with occasional guests on it. But he was fundamentally, he wanted to be a trio piano player and he fundamentally was. So nobody messed with him artistically too much that way.
